opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated levers we have right now. For a long time the mindset was: researchers design the model, and then systems people figure out how to make it run fast. But the hardware has very specific characteristics, and if you ignore them when you design the architecture, you leave a huge amount of performance on the table.

The key thing to understand about inference, especially decoding, is that it's mostly memory-bound, not compute-bound. When you generate one token at a time, you're loading all the weights and the KV cache from memory just to do a relatively small amount of arithmetic. Modern GPUs have enormous compute throughput, and memory bandwidth hasn't grown nearly as fast. So the GPU spends a lot of time waiting on data.

Once you see it that way, a lot of architecture decisions start to look like hardware decisions. Take attention. Multi-query attention and grouped-query attention are, at heart, about shrinking the KV cache so you move fewer bytes per token. More recent variants, like latent attention, push that further. They're designed so the decoding step does more arithmetic per byte loaded, which matches what the hardware is good at. Same story with state space models and linear attention variants like Mamba: you replace a KV cache that grows with sequence length with a fixed-size state, so inference cost per token stays constant. That's an architectural choice motivated by memory, not just by modeling quality.

It goes the other way too. FlashAttention didn't change the math of attention at all. It just restructured the computation to respect the memory hierarchy, keeping things in fast on-chip SRAM instead of constantly going back to HBM. That experience taught me that the "cost" of an operation isn't the FLOP count. It's how it maps onto the hardware. So when we design new layers now, we ask early on: can this be expressed as big matrix multiplies that use the tensor cores? Can it be chunked so it fits in SRAM? Will it parallelize well? If the answer is no, it probably won't win in practice, even if it looks elegant on paper.

Quantization and low precision are another good example. Hardware vendors are adding support for FP8 and FP4, and models that are trained or designed to be robust at those precisions get large speedups almost for free. That's co-design: the model adapts to what the chip does well, and the chip designers watch which formats the models actually use.

Speculative decoding and multi-token prediction fit the same pattern. Decoding underutilizes compute, so you spend that spare compute generating or verifying several tokens at once. You're turning a memory-bound problem into something closer to compute-bound.

So my view is that the best architectures over the next few years won't simply be the ones with the best perplexity per parameter. They'll be the ones with the best quality per unit of wall-clock time and per dollar on real hardware. Getting there means the people designing models and the people designing kernels and chips need to talk to each other much earlier in the process. That's a lot of what I find exciting about this area.

r001.rationale: The response connects hardware constraints, especially memory bandwidth, to architecture choices and says model and systems designers should work together early to address them.

r002.rationale: It says FlashAttention restructures attention to keep data in on-chip SRAM instead of repeatedly accessing HBM, clearly identifying reduced memory access as its approach.

r003.rationale: It mentions latent attention and more arithmetic per byte, but does not explain that DeepSeek’s multi-head latent attention projects the KV cache into a smaller latent space.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core idea is that the hardware isn't a fixed thing you just write software for. When you're designing an architecture, you really want to ask: what does this chip actually want to do? And GPUs, in particular, are extremely good at one thing, which is dense matrix multiplication. They have these specialized units, the tensor cores, that give you an enormous amount of compute, and almost everything else, memory bandwidth, moving data around, is comparatively slow and scarce.

So when I look at inference, the first thing I think about is where the time is actually going. For a lot of workloads, especially at long context with standard attention, you're not compute-bound at all. You're bound by moving the KV cache in and out of memory. The arithmetic is cheap; the memory traffic is expensive. Once you internalize that, it changes how you design the model. You start asking, can I reduce how much state I need to read per token? That's part of the motivation behind things like Mamba and state space models, where the state is fixed-size instead of growing with the sequence. It's also why you see grouped-query attention, multi-head latent attention, and so on, all of which are really just ways of shrinking what you have to load from memory.

The second direction is making the architecture match the shape of the hardware. FlashAttention came out of that kind of thinking, really. The algorithm wasn't new math, it was about reorganizing the computation so that you stay in fast on-chip memory as much as possible and avoid writing the big attention matrix out to HBM. That's a pure systems insight, but it has architectural consequences, because once attention is cheap you can afford longer contexts, and the model design changes in response.

And then there's the feedback loop going the other way, where architecture informs hardware. If model designers converge on certain operations, chip makers will build for them. We've seen that with lower-precision formats, FP8 and now FP4, which only make sense because people have figured out how to train and run models that tolerate them. The hardware and the algorithms are kind of co-evolving.

I'd say the general lesson is that a lot of the inefficiency in inference comes from a mismatch: a model designed in the abstract, running on hardware with very particular constraints. If you design with those constraints in mind from the start, you can get large speedups without changing what the model is capable of. And honestly, I think we're still early. Most architectures today are still shaped by what was convenient to train in 2017, not by what's efficient to serve in 2026.

r001.rationale: The response says to identify where inference time goes, notes that standard attention is often bottlenecked by moving the KV cache through memory, and explains that hardware constraints guide architecture and algorithm design.

r002.rationale: It describes FlashAttention as reorganizing computation to stay in fast on-chip memory and avoid writing the large attention matrix to HBM, reducing memory traffic.

r003.rationale: The response mentions multi-head latent attention as a way to shrink what must be loaded from memory, but does not explain projecting the KV cache into a smaller latent space.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that fewer FLOPs doesn’t necessarily mean lower latency. You have to think about where the data lives, how much you’re moving it, and whether the operations map well to the hardware.

Attention is a good example. You can keep the same mathematical operation but change how you compute it—doing more work while the data is in fast memory instead of repeatedly moving it back and forth. That can make it much faster without changing the model itself.

Then you can take that thinking into architecture design. During autoregressive generation, for example, the model has to keep reading a growing KV cache. So you might design an architecture that shares keys and values across heads, or uses a fixed-size state. Those choices change the memory requirements, but they also affect model quality, so you need to evaluate both together.

For me, that’s the value of co-design: you don’t design the model, freeze it, and only then ask someone to make it fast. You use what you learn from implementing and measuring it on hardware to guide the architecture itself.

r001.rationale: The response connects hardware-aware implementation and measurement to architecture choices, and identifies data movement and hardware fit as considerations that should guide redesign.

r002.rationale: It describes computing attention in fast memory to reduce repeated data movement, but does not identify FlashAttention or clearly attribute that approach to it.

r003.rationale: It mentions sharing keys and values across heads or using fixed-size state, but not reducing KV-cache size by projecting it into a smaller latent space.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that fewer FLOPs doesn’t necessarily mean lower latency. You have to think about where the data lives, how much you’re moving between different levels of memory, and whether the operations map well to the hardware.

So you can approach it from both directions. Given an architecture, you can design better algorithms and kernels to run it efficiently. But you can also change the architecture so that the expensive parts become operations the hardware is good at. Those changes give you a much larger design space than optimizing either side independently.

For inference, the workload matters a lot, too. Processing a prompt and generating one token at a time have different bottlenecks. An architecture that’s efficient for one isn’t automatically efficient for the other. So I’d want that feedback loop: build the model, measure it on the hardware under the serving conditions you care about, and use those measurements to inform the next architecture.

r001.rationale: The response connects hardware-aware algorithm and architecture design to bottlenecks such as data movement and explains that algorithms or architectures can be changed to suit the hardware.

r002.rationale: It discusses memory movement generally but does not identify FlashAttention or say it reduces memory access.

r003.rationale: It does not mention DeepSeek, multi-head latent attention, or reducing KV-cache size through a smaller latent space.
